title: Report on the Exchange Study Abroad at the University of Adelaide
paragraphs: I was given the opportunity to study abroad for 12 weeks at the University of Adelaide in South Australia. I would like to report, in part, what I felt and learned through the study abroad.

Adelaide is a city in the south of Australia facing the Southern Ocean. Perhaps because it was originally a colonial city planned for immigrants, many immigrants and their descendants live there, and when you walk around town you meet people of various origins. The English you hear also varies in pronunciation and accent from person to person, and it was an easy city to live in even for international students. It is also rich in nature: colorful parrots and pelicans fly even in town, and on holidays you can see wild koalas and kangaroos in the hills and fields in the suburbs.

The University of Adelaide does not have an affiliated hospital like Nagoya University Hospital, and medical students do clerkships at surrounding associated hospitals. I did all 12 weeks of my clerkship at the Royal Adelaide Hospital (RAH), next to the medical school headquarters. It is the largest hospital in South Australia, in a new building that had been relocated only two years earlier.

The first six weeks were in medical oncology, and the latter six weeks in gastroenterology. A supervising teacher is assigned, but basically every day I went to the ward at 8 a.m. and did ward work (history-taking, charting, blood sampling and so on) with the other students and residents. I also observed outpatient clinics and tests several times a week. The indications and regimens for chemotherapy drugs were broadly the same as in Japanese clinical practice, while for commonly used drugs such as antibiotics and anticoagulants there were many occasions when drugs different from Japan's were used, which was a good opportunity to think again about "why this drug is used."

At the beginning of the clerkship there were only unfamiliar and unknown things, but the local students, the doctors and the hospital staff were very kind to me and looked after me well. For example, when I was in trouble not knowing how to draw blood or how to write on paper charts, students and residents taught me step by step. When taking histories from patients or their families whose English was hard to understand, students often came along with me each time. For about the first month I only observed, but as I got used to it I was allowed to take histories, draw blood and do simple tests, which was stressful on the one hand and, on the other, encouragement to keep studying.

During the clerkship there was a coffee break almost every day, which left a strong impression. They valued taking breaks even when busy, and sometimes would deliberately interrupt rounds and go not to the hospital but to the cafe in the neighboring research building. During breaks everyone relaxed with their favorite drink in hand, and I could hear all sorts of stories even from doctors who usually seemed busy. Having a place every day to take time to ask questions and chat was, looking back, a great luxury. Contrary to my expectations, everyone knew a lot about Japanese culture, and when they told me about holidays in Japan and about Japanese food, I somehow felt inexplicably happy.

Looking back on the clinical clerkship in Adelaide after returning to Japan, I realise anew the differences between Australia and Japan in the clinical setting, medical education and values. At RAH, the average age of patients is young (only 30% are 65 or older), so patients are often discharged soon. In conferences, because patients' races, places of origin and lifestyles are very diverse, they place importance on place of origin and life history when deciding the differential diagnosis and treatment, and since I had not thought much about this in the polyclinic clerkships until then, it was fresh to me. I also think that medical education is not education that prioritises the acquisition of knowledge, as in the Japanese polyclinic clerkship, but education that makes you ready to contribute immediately after becoming a doctor. Through the study abroad, I feel that I have become able to think about the medical knowledge and clinical setting that I learn in Japan from another perspective.

Finally, I thank the people of the International Collaboration Office who supported the advance negotiations and preparations for studying abroad, and the people of the University of Adelaide and RAH who accepted me for clinical clerkships. Thank you.
